title: A quits-based labour signal puts US wage pressure near its historical average
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: The Heise–Pearce–Weber indicator placed US labour-market pressure on wages very close to its historical average in November 2025. Its monthly reading was −0.01, expressed in standard deviations from the reference mean. A reading near zero does not mean wages have stopped rising. It means the combination of vacancies, effective job search and quits has returned to the centre of its historical range, after substantial easing between 2022 and 2024. For a rates investor, the article's central contribution is a test of which measures can help anticipate next quarter's private-sector wage growth. The authors provide evidence about wages, without giving a policy rate forecast or asserting that a particular level of wage growth is consistent with the Fed's inflation objective.

The idea begins with workers who already have jobs. Employers competing to recruit them can face wage pressure that a measure based on vacancies divided by unemployed people misses. The quits rate captures workers' willingness or ability to leave existing positions, while vacancies per effective searcher includes both people out of work and those seeking a move from employment. The authors combine these two measures, weighting them with the coefficients of a regression of wage growth on both. Quits and vacancies come from JOLTS and the set of effective searchers is constructed from the Current Population Survey. A composite built this way can distinguish a change in posted openings from a change accompanied by movement among employed workers.

The first chart compares the index to the three-month percentage change in the Employment Cost Index for the wages and salaries of private-industry workers. Both measures are standardised; the vertical distance between lines is not a difference in wage inflation measured in percentage points. The quarterly chart runs from 1994 through the third quarter of 2025. A separate monthly index starts in December 2000 and extends to November 2025. The monthly series uses the coefficients fitted at quarterly frequency, because the ECI is released quarterly. It offers a more frequent reading of one set of explanatory variables. It does not supply a newly observed monthly ECI. Both panels show the exceptional post-pandemic rise and subsequent decline. Their recent flattening helps distinguish the level of current pressure from its earlier downward momentum.

The forecasting exercise asks a harder question than whether the series look alike historically. Starting with 2004:Q1, the authors use information available through the preceding quarter to predict the following quarter's three-month wage growth, then repeat the exercise through successive quarters. They compare forecasts derived from a range of tightness indicators with a simple model that predicts wage inflation using its own lag. The second chart displays root mean square forecast errors averaged over rolling windows described as forty quarters. A lower line means smaller errors; it conveys no information about whether a particular forecast was too high or too low. The comparison ends in 2024:Q4 because some alternative indicators are unavailable thereafter. The November 2025 reading is an update of the signal, outside the period for which this chart ranks the competing forecasts.

Before the pandemic the composite and the quits rate performed well, but several alternatives did nearly as well. The distinction became clearer in 2020. Errors rose markedly for many alternatives, including measures based on unemployment or job finding, while the composite and quits continued to perform better than the autoregressive benchmark. Toward the end of the comparison the composite has a modest advantage over quits alone. Vacancies per unemployed worker performed reasonably well until about 2015 before its relative forecasting record weakened. The authors relate that deterioration to a changing relationship between vacancies and other labour indicators (forecasting section).

The practical implication is to compare a monthly change in headline vacancies with evidence that workers are actually changing jobs and competing for those vacancies. The paper's evidence favours giving quits meaningful weight, particularly in the unusually large swings after 2020. It does not show that adding every ingredient of the composite improves the forecast in each quarter, and the gap relative to quits alone is much smaller than that relative to several vacancy-based measures. No estimate in the article translates a standardised index move directly into changes in services inflation, employer profit margins or a market-implied path for interest rates. Those require separate evidence about productivity, prices and policy.

questions.question: How much incremental forecasting information does the composite provide over quits alone?
questions.detail: The best two series look close for much of the sample, with a modest lead for the composite near the end. An investor trading an ECI surprise needs to know how often this alters the sign or size of the forecast. Use the Staff Report's competing specifications, forecast vintages and quarter-by-quarter errors to compare paired forecasts, including results outside the pandemic quarters.

questions.question: Can revisions or data-release lags change the signal available ahead of the ECI?
questions.detail: The note constructs a monthly indicator from surveys with different release schedules and applies quarterly regression weights. Its latest monthly observation extends beyond its comparative forecasting exercise. Reconstruct what could actually have been known ahead of each ECI release from dated CPS and JOLTS vintages, then compare first-release and revised index readings at turning points.

questions.question: When would average wage pressure still matter for inflation or earnings?
questions.detail: The source establishes a link to wage growth, while the step from wages to costs per unit of output remains open. For a rates or equity view, align the wage measure with productivity, labour shares and price-setting evidence in the relevant sectors. The ECI, official productivity releases and corporate margin disclosures would help test whether a wage surprise is absorbed by output gains, margins or selling prices.
